Drawing the field direction the wrong way, or not reading the poles from the field lines (Summer 2023 U7 Physics Booklet B Q1; Summer 2023 P2 H Q9)

workedExamples.stem:
An electromagnet is made from a coil of wire wound on a wooden rod and joined to a power supply.
State three ways to make it stronger. [3]

steps.decision: Say the quantity. 'A bigger power supply' names a part; the mark is for more current.

steps.working: Wind more turns of wire on the coil.
steps.decision: Every extra turn adds its own field to the others.

steps.working: Replace the wooden rod with a soft iron core.
steps.decision: Wood does nothing for the field; soft iron makes it much stronger.

options: Soft iron is magnetised strongly by the coil, and loses it when the current stops
Any longer rod makes the field stronger
Iron is a better conductor of electricity
whyMenu.explain: The core's material is what matters: soft iron becomes a strong magnet while the current flows and stops being one when it is switched off. A rod's length is not what the marks are for, and conducting electricity has nothing to do with it.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: More current; more turns; a soft iron core in place of the wood.

twin.stem: State three ways to make an electromagnet with a soft iron core weaker. [3]

accepted: less current, fewer turns, and remove the iron core

any: take out the soft iron core

steps.working: The field lines leave the left end, so the left end is a north pole.
steps.decision: Read the pole from the field first: lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole.

options.feedback: Right. Field lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole, and here they come out of the left end.
Field lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole, and here they come out of the left end. So the answer is a north pole.

steps.working: Seen from the left end, a north pole needs the current to flow anticlockwise.

options: Anticlockwise current makes the end you are looking at a north pole
Current always flows anticlockwise in a coil
The cell's long plate is on the left
whyMenu.explain: The end rule links the two: anticlockwise, seen from an end, makes that end north. Here the pole is known, so the rule is read backwards: north means anticlockwise.

options.feedback: Right. Seen from an end, anticlockwise current makes that end a north pole, so a north pole needs the current anticlockwise.
Seen from an end, anticlockwise current makes that end a north pole, so a north pole needs the current anticlockwise. So the answer is anticlockwise.

steps.working: From the left end the front of the coil is on your right, and anticlockwise there runs up the page: at X the current flows up.
steps.decision: Turn the end view into the side view: the side nearest you is on your right as you look along the coil from its left end.

options.feedback: Right. Looking along the coil from its left end, the front of the coil is on your right, and anticlockwise on the right-hand side runs upwards.
Looking along the coil from its left end, the front of the coil is on your right, and anticlockwise on the right-hand side runs upwards. So the answer is up the page.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Up the page at X: the left end is a north pole, so seen from it the current runs anticlockwise.

twin.stem: A coil's left-hand end is a south pole. Seen from that left-hand end, which way does the current flow?

options.feedback: Right. Seen from an end, clockwise current makes that end a south pole, so a south pole needs the current clockwise.
Seen from an end, clockwise current makes that end a south pole, so a south pole needs the current clockwise. So the answer is clockwise.

items.stem: Something you met in earlier science: which of these is attracted to a magnet?

options.feedback: Iron is a magnetic material: a magnet attracts it. That is why an iron core matters in an electromagnet.
Copper is a metal but not a magnetic material. Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are.
Plastic is not magnetic. Iron is.

items.stem: Two magnets are held with their north poles facing each other. What happens?

options.feedback: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
That happens with a north and a south pole. Two norths repel.
Poles always affect each other: like poles repel.

items.stem: From the topic on circuits: what is an electric current in a metal wire?

options.feedback: Right: and a current in a coil is what makes an electromagnet's field.
Protons stay in the atoms' nuclei. The current in a metal is a flow of electrons.

options.text: a store of energy in the wire
options.feedback: A current is a flow of charge: electrons moving through the wire.

items.stem: Outside a bar magnet, which way do its field lines point?

options.text: from the north pole to the south pole
options.feedback: Out of north, into south, outside the magnet.

options.text: from the south pole to the north pole
options.feedback: That is the wrong way round: outside the magnet they leave the north pole and enter the south pole.
A field has a direction, which is why every line needs an arrow: north to south outside.

items.stem: Iron filings sprinkled round a magnet show the field's shape. What can they not show?

options.feedback: Filings line up but have no north end, so they cannot show direction. A plotting compass can.
Filings bunch up where the field is strongest, so they do show that. What they cannot show is direction: that needs a compass.
The shape is exactly what they show. The direction is what they miss.

items.stem: Which of these would earn a mark for a way to make an electromagnet stronger?

options.feedback: Current, turns and a soft iron core are the three.
That names a part, not the quantity. Write 'increase the current'.
The mark is for the core's material (soft iron), not its size.

items.stem: Seen from one end of a coil, the current flows anticlockwise. Which pole is that end?

options.feedback: Anticlockwise from the end you are looking at: north.
Clockwise makes a south pole; anticlockwise makes a north pole.

A pupil makes an electromagnet by winding wire round a core and connecting it to a battery.

Fewer turns make a weaker field.

Without the soft iron core the field is much weaker.

context.setting: Counting the nails an electromagnet can hold

parts.stem:
A pupil investigates how the strength of an electromagnet depends on the current. She changes the current and counts how many iron nails it holds.
Identify the independent variable.
hints: The one she changes on purpose.
parts.workedSolution: The current: it is what she changes.

parts.stem: Identify the dependent variable.
hints: The one she measures (counts) each time.
parts.workedSolution: The number of nails the electromagnet holds: it is what she measures.

commonErrors.feedback: The current is the one she changes: the independent variable. The dependent variable is what she measures each time, the number of nails held.

parts.stem:
At one current the electromagnet held 16 nails in the first test and 18 in the second.
Calculate the average number of nails held.
hints: Add the two counts, then divide by 2. An average must lie between the two counts.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides only the second count by 2: 16 + 18 ÷ 2. Add first, then divide: (16 + 18) ÷ 2 = 17. An average bigger than both counts should look wrong straight away.

parts.stem:
Decreasing the current decreases the strength of the electromagnet.
State two other ways of decreasing its strength.

accepted: fewer turns on the coil, and remove the iron core

any: take out the soft iron core

hints: Current is taken: that leaves the coil and the core.
parts.workedSolution: Use fewer turns of wire on the coil; take out the iron core.

commonErrors.feedback: Name the quantity, not the part. A smaller battery, or one fewer cell, earns nothing on its own: write 'decrease the current'. Summer 2025 examiners found most answers talked about the battery and lost these marks.

It is the core's material that the marks are for, not its size: a soft iron core makes the electromagnet stronger, and taking it out makes it weaker. Summer 2025 examiners saw many answers change the core's dimensions instead.

context.setting: Checking a partner's notes on a bar magnet's field

parts.stem:
Ruth checks four sentences her partner wrote about the field of a bar magnet.
Which sentence is wrong?

options.text: A plotting compass's north end points along the field line.
options.feedback: That one is right: the needle lines up with the field, its north end pointing the way the field goes. The wrong sentence is the one with the field running from south to north.

options.text: The field lines are closest together near the poles.
options.feedback: That one is right: the field is strongest at the poles, where the lines crowd together. The wrong one has the field running from south to north outside the magnet.

options.text: Outside the magnet, the field lines run from the south pole to the north pole.
options.feedback: Right: that one is backwards. Outside a magnet the field runs from the north pole to the south pole.

options.text: Field lines never cross each other.
options.feedback: That one is right: at each point the field has only one direction, so two lines cannot cross. The wrong one has the field running from south to north outside the magnet.

scheme.for: the sentence that has the field running from south to north outside the magnet

hints: Check each sentence against the bar magnet in the note: the direction, the crowding, the crossing and the compass.
parts.workedSolution: The third sentence is wrong: outside a bar magnet the field lines run from the north pole to the south pole.

context.setting: Steel washers lifted by a coil on a cardboard tube

parts.stem:
Aidan winds wire on a cardboard tube and joins it to a power supply. He keeps the current the same, changes the number of turns, and counts how many steel washers the coil lifts each time.
Identify the independent variable.
hints: The one he changes on purpose.
parts.workedSolution: The number of turns: it is what he changes.

parts.stem: Identify the dependent variable.
hints: The one he counts each time.
parts.workedSolution: The number of washers the coil lifts: it is what he counts.

commonErrors.feedback: The number of turns is the one he changes: the independent variable. The dependent variable is what he counts each time, the number of washers lifted.

parts.stem:
With 40 turns the coil lifted 11 washers in the first test and 15 in the second.
Calculate the average number of washers lifted.
hints: Add the two counts, then divide by 2. An average must lie between the two counts.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides only the second count by 2: 11 + 15 ÷ 2. Add first, then divide: (11 + 15) ÷ 2 = 13. An average bigger than both counts should look wrong straight away.

parts.stem:
Adding turns makes the electromagnet stronger.
State two other ways of making it stronger.

accepted: increase the current, and put a soft iron core in the tube

scheme.for: put a (soft) iron core in the coil

hints: Turns are taken: that leaves the current and what is inside the coil.
parts.workedSolution: Increase the current; put a soft iron core inside the cardboard tube.

commonErrors.feedback: Name the quantity, not the part. A bigger battery, or an extra cell, earns nothing on its own: write 'increase the current'. Summer 2025 examiners found most answers talked about the battery and lost these marks.

It is the core's material that the marks are for, not its size: a soft iron core makes the electromagnet stronger, and taking it out makes it weaker. Summer 2025 examiners saw many answers change the core's dimensions instead.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows one end of a coil, seen straight on. This end is a south pole.
Which way does the current flow round this end?

options.feedback: Right: seen from a south pole, the current runs clockwise.
Anticlockwise would make this end a north pole. The end rule works both ways: a south pole needs the current clockwise, seen from that end.

options.text: it cannot be told from the pole
options.feedback: The end rule works backwards too: a south pole means the current runs clockwise, seen from that end.

hints: Anticlockwise makes a north pole. What does a south pole need?
parts.workedSolution: Clockwise: seen from a south pole, the current runs clockwise.

parts.stem: Inside the coil, which way does the magnetic field point?

options.feedback: Right: inside a coil the field runs from the south end to the north end, so each field line is a closed loop.
That is the direction outside the coil. Inside, the field runs the other way, from the south end to the north end, closing each loop.

options.text: there is no field inside the coil
options.feedback: The field inside a coil is strong and even: straight lines running from the south end to the north end.

scheme.for: towards the north end (from south to north inside the coil)

hints: Outside, the lines go from north to south. Each line is a closed loop: which way must it run inside?
parts.workedSolution: Towards the north end: inside the coil the field runs from the south end to the north end.

parts.stem:
A pupil connects a coil of wire on a soft iron core to a cell to make an electromagnet.
Give three changes that would make this electromagnet weaker.

accepted: decrease the current, use fewer turns, and remove the soft iron core

any: take out the soft iron core

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025: most answers dealt with the battery (removing it or some cells) or changed the core's size, and lost these marks.

hints: The opposite of the three ways that make it stronger.
parts.workedSolution: Decrease the current; wind fewer turns of wire; take out the soft iron core.

commonErrors.feedback: Name the quantity, not the part. A smaller battery, or one fewer cell, earns nothing on its own: write 'decrease the current'. Summer 2025 examiners found most answers talked about the battery and lost these marks.

It is the core's material that the marks are for, not its size: a soft iron core makes the electromagnet stronger, and taking it out makes it weaker. Summer 2025 examiners saw many answers change the core's dimensions instead.

parts.stem: What would you place near the electromagnet to find which way its field points?
hints: Its needle lines up with the field.
parts.workedSolution: A plotting compass.

parts.stem: The diagram shows the coil and some of its field lines. Which end of the coil is its north pole?

options.feedback: Field lines leave a north pole, and here they come out of the left end.
Follow the arrows: the lines come out of the left end and go into the right end. Lines leave a north pole, so the left end is north.

scheme.for: the left end (the field lines leave it)

hints: Field lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole.
parts.workedSolution: The left end: the field lines come out of it.

parts.stem: The cell is turned round. What happens to the poles?

options.text: the north and south poles swap ends
options.feedback: The current reverses, so every field arrow reverses and the poles swap.

options.text: the poles stay where they are
options.feedback: Turning the cell round reverses the current, and that reverses the field: the poles swap ends.

options.text: the coil stops being a magnet
options.feedback: A current still flows, just the other way, so the coil is still a magnet with its poles swapped.

hints: Reversing the current reverses the field.
parts.workedSolution: The north and south poles swap ends.

findTheMistake.stem:
Seán tests an electromagnet twice at the same current. It holds 22 nails, then 26 nails. He is asked for the average number of nails held.
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is typed without brackets, so only the 26 is divided by 2. Add the two counts first, then divide: (22 + 26) ÷ 2. An average of 35 is more than either count, which cannot be right.
findTheMistake.feedback: An average always lies between the numbers it comes from: 24 lies between 22 and 26, 35 does not. Unit 7 examiners (Summer 2024, the biology practical in Booklet A) saw averages typed as A + B / 2, and asked candidates to check that the result looks reasonable.

prompts.prompt: Which way do field lines point outside a bar magnet?
prompts.answer: From the north pole to the south pole.

prompts.prompt: Name three ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
prompts.answer: More current, more turns on the coil, and a soft iron core.

prompts.prompt: What happens to a coil's poles when its current is reversed?
prompts.answer: They swap ends: the field keeps its shape but every arrow reverses.

prompts.prompt: What instrument shows the direction of a magnetic field?
Seen from one end of a coil, the current runs anticlockwise. Which pole is that end?
prompts.answer: A north pole; clockwise would make it a south pole.
